title: Private security has become public-safety infrastructure while its workforce remains underpaid and underprotected
source_unit: UC Berkeley Labor Center, Underpaid, Undervalued, and Essential: The Security Guard Workforce in the United States, July 2026; national data and state/metropolitan factsheet synthesis
geography: United States; national security-guard workforce with selected state and metropolitan comparisons

annual_openings.unit: projected openings per year, mostly replacement openings

contract_security_share.unit: percent working for contract security firms rather than the establishments protected

workforce_public_role.value: guards staff hospitals, schools, transit systems, stores, and offices and increasingly de-escalate conflicts, manage emergencies, and respond to mental-health crises

observations.method: Synthesis of national labor-market data with UC Berkeley Labor Center state and metropolitan security-workforce factsheets.
observations.uncertainty: The workforce and openings are reported industry estimates/projections; replacement openings do not by themselves measure vacancy duration, service quality, or unmet public-safety need.
observations.subgroup: U.S. private security officers, including contract and directly employed guards.
observations.counterinterpretation: Private security staffing varies by site, contract, technology, policing, local regulation, and demand; a large workforce does not mean every guard performs the same public-safety role.

denominator.unit: U.S. security officer workforce comparison universe

relative_wage.unit: cents earned by a median security officer per dollar earned by the typical U.S. worker

below_mit_living_wage.unit: percent earning below the MIT living wage for a single adult

low_wage_benchmark.unit: percent classified as low-wage under a two-thirds-of-median benchmark

observations.method: Labor-market wage, living-wage, and benefits analysis presented by the Berkeley Labor Center.
observations.uncertainty: Benchmarks vary by location, household size, hours, benefits, and overtime; median earnings do not establish take-home pay, schedule stability, or household poverty.
observations.subgroup: U.S. security officers, with demographic and geography differences reported separately.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some guards receive overtime, public benefits, household support, or employer benefits not captured by the headline wage comparison; local wages may exceed or fall below the national median.

denominator.unit: U.S. security-industry workforce and regulatory comparison universe

training_hours_range.value: 4 to 48 hours among states with minimums

fatality_risk.value: more than twice the average worker rate

fatal_assault_share.unit: share of fatal injuries resulting from assaults

observations.method: National industry turnover and occupational-safety data combined with review of state licensing and training requirements.
observations.uncertainty: Turnover definitions, occupational classifications, injury reporting, and state training rules differ; the report does not identify a single causal effect of wages, training, contracting, or site conditions on each outcome.
observations.subgroup: Security guards and unarmed-guard regulatory systems across the United States.
observations.counterinterpretation: Turnover can reflect seasonal work, labor-market alternatives, site closure, voluntary mobility, or workers moving into better jobs; training hours are not equivalent to training quality.

denominator.unit: report synthesis of security-workforce and public-safety evidence

job_quality_service_link.value: higher pay and lower turnover are associated with better and more reliable security services; constant churn erodes experience and readiness

policy_route.value: sectoral pay and benefit standards, standardized training, responsible contracting, and career pathways

institutional_mechanism.value: low-bid contracting can externalize labor costs while transferring readiness and safety risk to workers, sites, and the public

observations.method: Report synthesis of security-industry research, labor standards, contracting structures, and the San Francisco International Airport case cited by the authors.
observations.uncertainty: The report does not provide a unified causal estimate across all sites or prove that each proposed intervention will improve public safety in every setting.
observations.subgroup: Security officers, contracting firms, protected establishments, and members of the public using sites staffed by private security.
observations.counterinterpretation: Technology, site design, management, policing, public investment, and local conditions also shape security reliability; higher pay alone is not a complete safety strategy.

related_sources.claim: Direct PDF of the national report, methods, tables, references, and policy analysis.
Berkeley Labor Center series page for state and metropolitan security-workforce factsheets.

boundary: This record identifies a U.S. infrastructure-and-labor mechanism in which private security has expanded into frontline public-safety work while low wages, thin benefits, high turnover, uneven training, and elevated injury risk weaken workforce stability. It does not establish that any single job-quality intervention causes a specific safety outcome, nor that all private security sites have the same conditions.
